clue.text: Last mad daring involved in horrendous battle

indicators.note: Someone mad is deranged, out of their right mind, and the letters beside the word come out just as deranged.
An involved story is a tangled one, and tangled letters no longer keep the sequence they were handed over in.

parts.note: four letters of raw material, taken exactly as they stand
six more letters, to be jumbled together with the first four

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a report of one last reckless act, and the two words that sound most like description, mad and involved, are both instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the six-month siege of 1942-43 was among the deadliest fights in history, so the city's name stands for one horrendous battle.

clue.text: Exploit you reserve for films

parts.note: a feat is an exploit, a deed worth telling people about
the letter U does duty for 'you', the way a text message does
res. is how reserve is written on a team sheet or a booking

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here looks like an instruction, because all three pieces are ordinary words taken at face value and the surface stays a sentence about a film collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A feature is a full-length cinema picture as opposed to a short, so the plural names exactly what a programme at the pictures is made of.

clue.text: A second attempt to fix a wrong

indicators.note: To fix something is to fasten it in place, and what is fastened in ends up inside rather than alongside.

parts.note: the clue's opening A, taken as a single letter
S is the second on a stopwatch
an attempt at something is a try at it
the clue's other a, again a letter at face value

explanation.walkthrough: 'A wrong' at the end wants to be a noun, an injustice somebody has to put right; the definition is the last word on its own, and it is an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: To go astray is to wander off the right path, morally or literally, which is 'wrong' as an adverb rather than as a name for an injustice.

clue.text: Plant conifer, not houses

indicators.note: A house holds its occupants within its walls, so the word is saying something sits lodged inside the letters beside it.

parts.note: four consecutive letters run straight across the comma, beginning inside the tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant conifer' reads as an instruction from a gardening column, which is what stops you noticing that a second, smaller plant is sitting inside the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferns are the feathery non-flowering growths that spread by spores, so the general word covers them as one instance of a plant.

clue.text: Time to wear first shoe? Capable of operating independently

indicators.note: What you wear sits on you rather than beside you, so the letter named first is put on inside the rest of the build.

parts.note: a sandal is a shoe, and this one opens up after its first letter
first is number one, written as a label the way 'take one' is
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.walkthrough: 'First shoe' is written the way a label is, shoe number one, and the question mark is the setter owning that liberty; the surface is just somebody getting dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A standalone machine runs on its own without being plugged into a larger system, which is exactly the capability the definition spells out.

clue.text: Troy protected by unscrupulous Olympian

indicators.note: A guard stands all round whatever it protects, so the letter named before goes inside the word named after.

parts.note: someone unscrupulous has no morals, and the word parts near its end
t is the abbreviation for troy, the system of weights gold and silver are sold by

explanation.walkthrough: Troy is capitalised to look like the besieged city, and the classical surface helps: an Olympian here is a god of the mountain, not an athlete at the games.
explanation.definitionFit: The Olympians are the deathless gods of Greek myth, so a being who never dies is one of them, with the athletic sense left as the decoy.

clue.text: Good advice in most of cricket book, offering much for openers

indicators.note: Most of a word is the bulk of it and not all, so the tail is left behind — loosely used here, since two letters go rather than the usual one.

parts.note: Wisden is the fat yellow almanack that has recorded every first-class cricket match since 1864, and it hands over the greater part of itself

indicators.note: 'For openers' means 'to begin with', and what begins a word is its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words, in the order they come

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a review praising a cricket annual, and 'for openers' does double duty: batting slang in the picture, an instruction in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Not just knowledge but sound judgement handed to somebody else, which is what good advice is when it turns out to be worth taking.

clue.text: Turning up, agreed to accept kiss: so exciting

indicators.note: In a down entry up runs from the bottom towards the top, so a word turned that way is read back along the column.
To accept something is to take it in, so these letters part and let the next one sit among them.

parts.note: agreed is yes, set climbing up the column
X is the kiss at the foot of a letter

explanation.walkthrough: Kiss meaning X is one of the first conventions worth learning, and the colon does the joining: everything before it builds, everything after it defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond the erotic sense the adjective is everyday praise for anything thrillingly attractive, the way a sexy idea is an exciting one.

clue.text: One of perhaps 16 having short nap — couldn't be shorter

indicators.note: 'Perhaps' flags an example: the age given is one instance of the word wanted, not the word itself.
Something short has had its end cut off, so the word beside this hands over everything but its final letter.

parts.note: a sixteen-year-old is one of the teens, the years from thirteen to nineteen
a siesta is the afternoon nap, docked of its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: The bare 16 looks like a cross-reference to another entry in the grid. It is only the number, and the age it names is the whole point.
explanation.definitionFit: Teensiest is the playful superlative of teensy, as small as a thing can get, and a thing that could not be shorter is exactly that.

clue.text: Here's Augusta: important, second in Georgia

definitions.note: The definition is a pointer rather than a synonym: Augusta is a seat of government, and the answer is the place you would be standing in if you were there.

parts.note: the main issue is the important one

indicators.note: Second in a word means its second letter, counted from the front — one letter only, not an abbreviation of the whole thing.

parts.note: the second letter of that state's name, and nothing else of it

explanation.walkthrough: There is an Augusta in Georgia too, the home of the Masters, so the clue's own last word is the red herring and lends nothing but a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Augusta is the state capital of Maine, so the setter identifies the state by naming the town where its legislature sits.

clue.text: Behind sailors touring a palace

parts.note: a train running behind is running late

indicators.note: A tour goes right round its subject, so this pair of letters opens up and travels either side of what comes next.

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, the crossword's standard sailors
the clue's own a, taken as a single letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' opens the clue looking like the definition, a rear end, and turns out to be the first piece of the build instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lateran in Rome housed the popes for a thousand years before the Vatican did, so the general word names it by example.

clue.missingNote: What looks like a printing error is the whole trick: with no words to read, the only thing left pointing at the answer is the clue's own number. This is 12, and twelve o'clock is the middle of the day.

clue.text: Anxious, not at first very worried

indicators.note: A worried person frets and fidgets, and letters that fidget will not stay in the order they were given.
At first means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is wanted.

parts.note: the opening letter of 'not' and no more of it
four letters shaken out of the order they arrived in

explanation.walkthrough: In British use nervy means jumpy and on edge; an American reader hears the opposite, since over there a nervy move is a bold one.
explanation.definitionFit: Anxious and nervy are everyday British synonyms, both meaning on edge, though the same adjective in American English means brazen instead.

clue.text: Imogen has key to get back home for these regular occasions

indicators.note: Getting back is going the way you came, so those letters are read from the far end towards the front.

parts.note: Imogen is this puzzle's setter, and a setter naming herself in her own clue means ME
Alt is the key beside the space bar on every keyboard
a semi is a semi-detached house, the standard British suburban home, written the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: Setters sign their own clues more often than you would expect, and 'Imogen has' reads as a sentence about a person rather than an instruction to write two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mealtimes are the fixed points of the day at which people sit down to eat, so they are occasions that recur to a regular schedule.

clue.text: Old art of singing in church, energy dropping, intermittently lusty

indicators.note: E is the symbol for energy, and in a down entry a letter that drops falls to a lower place in the word rather than leaving it.

parts.note: a minster is a great church, as at York or Beverley, with its E fallen one place down the column

indicators.note: Something intermittent happens every so often instead of continuously, so the letters are picked at every other step.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the word, taken in turn

explanation.walkthrough: 'In church' looks like where the singing happens and is really the building's other name; the E is not deleted, it only shifts down a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The minstrel's craft, singing verse to a harp in a lord's hall, which makes it precisely an old art of singing.

clue.text: Talk about date followed by letter, quick way to seek a mate

definitions.text: quick way to seek a mate

indicators.note: One thing about another is wrapped round it, so the letter named next sits inside the word named first.
What follows comes after, so the final piece is written on the end rather than tucked inside.

parts.note: a talk given to an audience is a speech, and it splits after four letters
d is the standard abbreviation for date
ess is how the letter S is spelt out in full

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all online dating — talk, date, letter, seeking a mate — and the mate actually wanted is the one that ends a game at the board.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess played against a fast clock, and checkmate is the mate being sought, so the whole phrase describes the game rather than defining a word.

clue.text: Bad service aboard Trans-Siberian railway, say, a perilous enterprise

indicators.note: To come aboard is to get on board a train or a ship, and whatever is aboard travels inside it, not beside it.
'Say' means 'for instance', flagging that the line named is only one example of the broader thing the letters spell.

parts.note: the line from Moscow to Vladivostok is one such way across that country, and it opens up near the end
in tennis a let is a serve that clips the net and has to be taken again

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about a shabby train journey, so the definition at the end reads like more of the same description rather than the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning a revolver's cylinder and pulling the trigger is the byword for any venture that stakes everything on chance, which is as perilous as an enterprise gets.

clue.text: Working together, fit to join lineout

indicators.note: The rugby word breaks in half, and the second half is the instruction: something out of true is not as it should be, so these letters do not stand as they were handed over.

parts.note: an ague is a shivering fit of fever, so 'fit' is the seizure and not the adjective for healthy
the first four letters of the rugby set piece are the material to work on; the rest of the word is doing the other job

explanation.walkthrough: A lineout is the restart a player might be fit to join, and printing it as one word is what hides the seam: four letters of material, then the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in league with somebody is to be acting jointly with them, usually with a hint of conspiracy about it — working alongside, on the same side.

clue.text: Barrel carried by dog finally dropped? Shocking

indicators.note: The finally is the last letter, and dropping it leaves the word one letter shorter than it was.
Whatever is carried is held inside the carrier, so the first piece goes within the letters that follow.

parts.note: a terrier is a dog, docked here of its final letter
bl is the trade abbreviation for a barrel, the unit oil and beer are measured in

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a shaggy picture of a dog with a barrel at its collar, and 'dropped' sits inside it doing the work of an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are the everyday exaggeration for something appalling: a terrible mistake and a shocking mistake are the same mistake.

clue.text: Large quantity of drink: declare it bubbly

indicators.note: Bubbles rise and burst in no fixed order, so whatever is described as bubbly will not keep its letters where they were put.

parts.note: nine letters of raw material, taken from the two words together

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' is a noun in the surface — champagne, exactly the thing you might have to declare at customs — and an instruction in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten litres, so as a measure of anything drinkable it names a very large quantity indeed.

clue.text: Rich, so getting replacement for several groups of singers

indicators.note: A replacement takes over somebody else's place, and here every letter takes over somebody else's — a loose signal, but a signal of movement all the same.

parts.note: six letters of raw material, taken from both words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rich, so' does nothing in the surface beyond sounding like a wealthy man's excuse, and that is exactly what makes it hard to see as raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A choir is a body of singers performing together, so the plural names more than one such body — church, school or concert hall.

clue.text: Murderous monarch, one idolised by daughter

parts.note: the person a fan idolises is their hero
D is the family-tree abbreviation for daughter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a king adored by his own child, which is close to the opposite of the story the definition is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: Herod the Great ordered the killing of Bethlehem's infants in Matthew's gospel, so his name is the byword for a king who murders.

clue.text: Greeting wife, giving reverence

parts.note: hallo is the greeting, in the older spelling without an E
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverence' is a verb here rather than a noun, which is easy to miss: the definition is an action, and so is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hallow is to make or treat as holy, and 'reverence' used as a verb means to regard with that same deep respect.

clue.text: Sort of light worried baby

parts.note: neon is the gas in the tube, one sort of light among many
what's eating you? — to eat at somebody is to worry them

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary words used in their second sense, and neither the light nor the worry has anything to do with a nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: A newborn in its first few weeks, the medical term for the very youngest sort of baby there is.

clue.text: Kiss cheek

definitions.meaning: the teenage sense of the verb: to kiss and cuddle at length
British slang for brass-faced impudence, the nerve to ask for something outrageous

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses, and nothing at all between them — the shorter a double definition is, the harder it is to spot that it is one.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to kiss and canoodle; as a noun it is British slang for the brass-faced impudence that 'cheek' also names.

clue.text: Want to catch falcon regularly returning ravenous

indicators.note: Taken regularly means taken at a fixed interval, and the interval here is every other letter.
Returning is coming back the way you went, so those three letters are read from the last of them to the first.
To catch something is to have it in your grasp, so the longer word closes around the letters named next.

parts.note: a want is a wish, and the word opens after its first letter
the first, third and fifth letters of the bird, then turned round

explanation.walkthrough: The falconry surface is a decoy: the bird's name is there only to be raided for letters, and the definition is about appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: Ravenously hungry — to wolf your food is to bolt it down — so the adjective carries exactly that sense of insatiable appetite.

clue.text: Showed sorrow as all of us part

parts.note: all of us, speaking of ourselves, is we
pt is how part is abbreviated on a title page

explanation.walkthrough: 'As all of us part' reads as a leave-taking, and the definition belongs to the same picture, so the surface never once breaks character.
explanation.definitionFit: To weep is to shed tears, the plainest outward show of sorrow there is, and the past tense matches 'showed'.

clue.text: Island shivering in 4C?

indicators.note: A shiver is an uncontrollable shake, and shaken letters come to rest somewhere other than where they started.

parts.note: the numeral written out in letters, with the C of the temperature after it

explanation.walkthrough: A bare number in a Guardian clue usually points at another entry, and four degrees really would make you shiver; both readings are there to keep you off the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The northernmost of the Ionian islands off the Greek coast, so the general word names it by example.

clue.text: Dramatist's concession, filling gaps with a bit of comedy

parts.note: a sop is a small concession thrown to somebody to keep them quiet

indicators.note: What fills a space goes into it, so the letter named lands inside the word before it rather than after.

parts.note: gaps in a road or an argument are holes, and this word is prised open in the middle

indicators.note: A bit of a word is a fragment of it, and the smallest fragment a setter takes is the opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of comedy and nothing more of it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a playwright patching up a script, and the joke is buried in 'a bit of comedy': the man wrote tragedies.
explanation.definitionFit: He wrote Oedipus Rex and Antigone in fifth-century Athens, so the general word names him as one instance of the trade.
